utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Will you call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-01-48-PT, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon, counsel. For the Prosecution appear Mr. George David Hackney on my right-hand side, legal officer on my left-hand side Mr. Hasan Younis from trial support and myself Ekkehard Withopf, acting Senior Trial Attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Withopf. For the Defence? Excuse me. Could you turn the microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Bakir Caglar, Defence counsel for Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Kwon, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If my pronunciation is wrong, please correct me. Mr. Caglar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honour. C-a-g-l-a-r, Caglar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KREHO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, representatives of the Prosecution, and ladies and gentlemen from the Registry, I am Dijana Kreho, attorney from Bosnia-Herzegovina and assistant Defence counsel in this case. Ljiljana Kreho [As interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The previous trial ended a little bit late, so we had to start a little bit late accordingly due to the technical preparation. So my apologies on behalf of the Tribunal. This is the third Status Conference in this case held in accordance with Rule 65 bis, and the purpose of which is to review the status of the case and ensure its expeditious preparation for trial. Rule 65 bis (A) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence provides that a Status Conference shall be held within 120 days after the last Status Conference. However, I should say there has been a substantial delay after the last Status Conference which was held on the 12th of April. While more than 120 days have passed since the last Status Conference, I considered that it would be inappropriate to hold another Status Conference until now on the basis that the accused has challenged the appointment of his former counsel, that is Mr. Richard Soyer by the Registrar. Until that issue was resolved and bearing in mind that Mr. Halilovic was granted provisional release on 13th of December of last year and was not in detention, I considered that the accused would not be unduly prejudiced by the holding of a Status Conference beyond that date. That matter was resolved on 25th September when Mr. Caglar was appointed as Defence counsel, and I thought that Mr. Caglar should be given at least a month of time to update himself with what has been going on with the trial. So that is the reason why we have -- we are having the third Status Conference today. Having said that, I would like to welcome Mr. Caglar and Mrs. Kreho, who have appeared at this Tribunal for the first time. And also, I would like to take this opportunity to express my thanks to Mr. Soyer, who tried to do his best as counsel for the interest of justice and also for the interest of the accused. I was impressed in particular by his sincere attitude in filing a motion for extension of time to file the Defence's pre-trial brief while at the same time requesting for withdrawal from the case. In this regard, I feel obliged to point out the following to the accused through his counsel: Let us say that the accused is allowed to challenge the appointment of a counsel by the Registrar in one way or another, as was in this case. But I think Mr. Halilovic had gone too far when he wrote a letter to Mr. Soyer saying, I quote, "If you do continue to act as if you were my counsel against my will and consent, I intend to inform the Austrian bar association and the media about your unethical behaviour." Mr. Soyer was appointed and paid by this Tribunal and thus he is duty-bound to act as a Defence counsel unless his appointment is withdrawn. Therefore, if the accused is not happy with the counsel appointed by the Tribunal, then he should address the issue to the Court rather than making such an impolite and I would say somewhat rude comments directly to the counsel. So it should be borne in mind that such an event should not take place again in the future. Now I will turn to the issues to be dealt with today, and there are a number of matters to be discussed during this conference relating to the preparation of the case for trial. First I will deal with disclosure issues first and then matters related to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, and finally matters relating to the Defence pre-trial brief. So first of all, I wonder if all the materials which were disclosed to Mr. Balijagic, former counsel, have now been transferred or disclosed to Mr. Caglar. So what is the current position, and there is any problem, Mr. Caglar?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have still not received --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have still not received them. It's not working? Yes it is. It's working now. I'm sorry. It's been switched off. I have still not received them. It's working now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's working.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have still not received the necessary documents. But before saying that to you, I need to apologise on behalf of Mr. Sefer Halilovic for this letter which he sent. I think he will correct this error that he has made, and I have advised him to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us the reason why you were not able to receive those materials? I think you were appointed a month ago, and I think you probably had an opportunity to pick the materials up in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I have not had the opportunity to review those documents. I'm saying this in French because there is a lack of communication between Bosnia and Istanbul, and these difficulties were also noted by Mr. Soyer. These are difficulties that need to be overcome, and I'm wondering what one can do, because I have not been able to get in touch with people who could help me. Mr. Faruk Balijagic, I have been trying to contact him but he has not replied. I think he has the necessary documents, but I'm wondering why he doesn't wish to communicate them to me. I think that I'll have to be content with the documents that you have here in the court, the documents that were kindly provided to me by Mr. Soyer. He sent them to me. But I don't know whether they are complete, and I will verify. I will check this out. At present, I'm unable to say more than that because I am unable to get in touch with Mr. Faruk Balijagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mrs. Kreho, do you not have in your possession those materials which were disclosed to Mr. Balijagic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KREHO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Balijagic gave me, in May, some documents which he had received in the process of disclosure from the OTP. However, all those documents are in the Bosnian language, and ten days ago we started to have those documents translated. We need to translate them first, explain them, and send them to Mr. Caglar in French so that he can understand them. I can say that from Sarajevo we did send all the expert reports to Mr. Caglar for him to study them. We have sent them documents -- sent him documents linked to the pre-trial Defence brief, but we are encountering a great deal of problems because of translation. As soon as all the documents have been translated and we have informed Mr. Caglar to that effect, everything will be disclosed to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we need the French translation. Can you give me an observation on that matter, Mr. Withopf?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the statements we just received from Mr. Caglar and Ms. Kreho reflects the difficult situation on the Defence side, and it emphasises the need for both Your Honour and the senior legal officer assigned to the Trial Chamber to take care and to even more take care of their duties under Rule 65 ter. We are facing a very difficult situation, and these difficulties are somewhat outside the normal scope. As you mentioned, the last Status Conference is more than half a year ago. A 65 ter meeting took place in mid-May of this year. Since then, there was only one major development in trial preparation, namely the timely filing of the Prosecution pre-trial brief. In mid-June, in addition, the Prosecution was trying to continue to comply with the various complications under the Rules, in particular disclosure related obligations. On the Defence side, as you know, Your Honour, nothing, literally nothing happened other than what can be described as a total mess caused by the accused and his previous Defence counsel, Mr. Balijagic. To make it very clear, we are not talking about the new Defence counsel, our learned colleague Mr. Caglar. The Prosecution, however, wishes to take this opportunity to illustrate the very particular difficulties the Prosecution is facing in this case because of the somewhat unusual situation on the Defence side. Mid-May, previous Defence counsel, Mr. Balijagic, withdrew. End of May the accused requested Mr. Balijagic be replaced by Ms. Kreho. In June the Registrar decided to not assign Ms. Kreho because of a potential conflict of interest, but to assign Mr. Soyer as the new Defence counsel. Later on, as you already mentioned, the accused did not communicate with Mr. Soyer at all. He refused to communicate with him, and finally, at the end of September Mr. Caglar has been assigned. The Prosecution over months tried to get materials including Rule 68 materials being disclosed without any success. Defence counsel, Mr. Balijagic, did not keep agreements to pick such materials up or Mr. Soyer was not prepared to receive them due to the lack of cooperation on the accused's side. Due to the mess on the Defence side, negotiations on potential agreements could not be followed up. Search criteria for both Rule 68 and Rule 66(B) materials were not provided as promised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Withopf. We'll get to the issues and specifics, but my question was whether you have a French translation available or you disclosed the French translation to Mr. Balijagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: No. We only disclosed materials in B/C/S language and English language. There is no translation in French language available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You didn't even start the translation into French?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: No. Since we only got yesterday to know about the new assigned Defence counsel speaks French only. We had a meeting with Mr. Caglar yesterday night, and only at this point in time we detected that he's only able to speak French but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I must say, the same is true of the Chamber. Okay. Thank you. So one of the main purposes to appoint Mrs. Kreho as a kind of assistant counsel or a co-counsel is to assist the new counsel to be appointed, and in that capacity, and you were able to review the materials disclosed to Mr. Balijagic. Am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A part of it, Your Honour. I have to apologise. I don't know the customs in your court, the custom in your court. I belong to the Strasbourg court and I have acted there in the human rights court, and I apologise for not getting up. I don't have that habit in Strasbourg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No problem. But let me ask the direct question. In my Scheduling Order, I ordered the Defence counsel to file its pre-trial brief on or before the 23rd of December of this year. Do you think you can meet the deadline?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's more than reasonable because you have lost already a lot of time. So far a lot of time has been wasted, so I will do everything I can to prepare the brief. I will do my very best. Because the experience so far hasn't been too agreeable, if I might call it that, with the attorneys of Mr. Halilovic, and my intention is to make up for lost time. Excuse me. But of course I'm counting on the assistance of Madam Kreho to provide me with the necessary documents, and I hope that will be sufficient for me to be able to present my defence to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KREHO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can provide the professor with all the documents but they are in Bosnian. I'm not sure that Mr. Caglar will be able to understand the content of each and every document. As for the translation of those documents into French, we need a great deal of time. I will do everything in my power to fulfil my obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Caglar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an assistant at the university who speaks Bosnian very well, and I will take upon myself the translation. If I have the necessary documents in time, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That's good news at least. Then let's deal with some specific matters one by one. 66(A)(i) disclosure has been completed by disclosing 105 witness statements, accompanied in the indictment on confirmation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct. The 66(A)(i) disclosure is complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us the current status of this situation regarding 66(A)(ii) disclosure, that is statements of all witnesses to be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Regarding the 66(A)(ii) disclosure, the situation is as follows, Your Honour: We initiated searches with regard to the 95 witnesses listed in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief. These searches have been initiated a month ago. This is an ongoing task. However, it doesn't have priority, and it doesn't have priority because a trial date is not yet set. To be more concrete, too date we got only the results with regard to four witnesses and eight witnesses are currently on the way, the search with regard to eight witnesses currently under way. However, once the trial date is known, searches can be completed within a reasonable time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But there is no big deal or problem since all the witness statements are accompanied by the -- with the indictment. So it is -- all of them are disclosed already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The witness -- those witness statements are disclosed. I'm talking about previous witness statements as referred to in Rule 66(A)(ii).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is customarily called as prior witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I am afraid we are using some jargon like 66(A)(i) which will certainly sound strange to Mr. Caglar, but you will get accustomed to it soon. I would like to deal with this so-called reciprocal disclosure and disclosure of exculpatory material. I will read out some Rules for the convenience of Mr. Caglar. Rule 66(B) provides that: "The Prosecutor shall, on request, permit the Defence to inspect any books, documents, photographs and tangible objects in the Prosecutor's custody or control, which are material to the preparation of the defence or are intended for use by the Prosecutor as evidence at trial or were obtained from or belonged to the accused." In the meantime, Rule 68 states: "The Prosecutor shall, as soon as practicable, disclose to the defence the existence of material known to the Prosecutor which in any way tends to suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or may affect the credibility of the Prosecution evidence." In relation to this, former Defence counsel, Mr. Balijagic, had triggered reciprocal disclosure asking for all the documents relating to a particular group of documents or Seve files, and the Prosecution responded to this in its filing dated 24th of September that it has potential exculpatory material for disclose available and that the Seve files are ready for inspection pursuant to reciprocal discovery procedure codified in Rule 66(B). I would like to hear from the parties what the current position is and whether there have been any discussions between the parties. Who would speak first?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May the Prosecution please speak first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: As you quite correctly stated, previous Defence counsel has triggered reciprocal disclosure and the Prosecution is of the opinion that once triggered it cannot be revoked involving the result and involving Rule 66(C). Actually, a duty of the Defence to disclose and give the Prosecution the opportunity to inspect books, documents, and all the other items as mentioned in this Rule. The Prosecution offered inspection of two sets of materials comprised of some 3.800 pages of documents. It refers to the alleged status awareness of the accused and the files Your Honour was just mentioning, the so-called Seve files. These fall within the scope of Rule 66(B). We offered in May and June to Mr. Balijagic to inspect these documents, and again in August we offered to the then-Defence counsel Mr. Soyer to inspect these documents. None of the then-Defence counsel or members of their team actually showed up to inspect such materials. In addition, the Prosecution asked previous Defence counsel Mr. Balijagic to submit search criteria to identify materials that may fall under Rule 66(B). Again such criteria were promised. However, by previous Defence counsel, it has never been followed up. Yesterday we had a meeting with Mr. Caglar and Ms. Kreho. I specifically asked Mr. Caglar what his position would be with regard to reciprocal disclosure. He didn't feel to be in a position yesterday night to answer this question, and the Prosecution would like to know, as you, Your Honour, what the current Defence position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Caglar, do you have any observation to that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour. First of all, I am familiar with the Rules of the Tribunal and the Article that you have just cited from. Yesterday evening, I reviewed the materials from previous conferences, and I think I can provide all the necessary documents to the Prosecutor. In my opinion, there will be no problem. There is, however, a small problem, and that is what I just told Mr. -- the Prosecutor at our previous meeting. I didn't appreciate too much the language that was used at that conference. I think we need to be far more open, more frank between ourselves, and I think that we should respect the Rules. Maybe it is too strong a word, but I think a kind of friendship should be established instead of a latent or potential conflict which I have been able to take note of at previous conferences, that existed at previous conferences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I appreciate the Defence's attitude in their readiness to provide the documents in their custody to the Prosecution, but the real issue is that the Prosecution is ready to show -- allow the Defence to inspect the documents in their custody, and in doing so, they need your cooperation. Some -- you have to offer them a search word or anything like that. So do you have any plan to contact the Prosecution to inspect the documents which is called the Seve sub-files, if I'm right.So do you think it would be more proper at this moment to set a time limit or you can do it, for instance, voluntarily? Or you are not triggering the reciprocal disclosure any more?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would like to engage in this reciprocal disclosure. I have seen this file this afternoon. It was shown to me in the Office of the Prosecutor, and I wonder if I can take them with me to have them at home. It would be easier for me. And I appreciate what has been done so far, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the Prosecution could help with this matter. I don't think it's a matter of 1.000 pages or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two issues to address. First of all, Rule 66(B) only provides the inspection of such materials. And the second issue involved is the one you just mentioned. The Seve files only are comprised of some 3.800 pages of documents. For pure practical reasons, it's not possible to provide Defence with copies of such materials. And again, it's the only obligation of the Prosecution to provide for inspection of such materials. We will provide a room. We are happy to do so. We will provide the materials. If Defence counsel wish to make copies of the one or the other documents, we are certainly open to it, but the Prosecution is not in a position and is not obliged to provide copies of some thousands of pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It seems to me that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apology. The Defence -- oh yes, Mr. Caglar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but in my opinion, there is a principle, a primordial principle, and that is the equality of arms. I respect the Rules of this Tribunal, but what is of primordial importance is the equality of arms between the Defence and the Prosecution. If they do not intend to communicate to me these files because of the enormity of those files, I wonder why then the Defence shouldn't do the same thing the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Rules of Procedure and Evidence does not provide the disclosure of copies of the documents in case of Rule 66(B), that is reciprocal disclosure. It only says that: "The Prosecution shall --" I'm sorry, "-- permit the Defence to inspect such documents." So it is if the Defence counsel wishes to have a reciprocal disclosure, it is their duty to go to the -- to contact the Prosecutor and inspect the documents in their custody themselves. So I would like to advise you to stay a little bit longer after this adjournment to have a discussion with the Prosecution and find a suitable way to doing that kind of disclosure. Having said that, let's move on to another issue. Let me deal with the Prosecution's pre-trial brief first. First of all, I would like to, as you, Mr. Withopf, mentioned, I would like to thank the Prosecution team for their submitting their pre-trial brief in due time, and it was well organised. I would like to congratulate that. According to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, it is my understanding that the Prosecution is planning to present 52 live witnesses and 43 92 bis witnesses and around 130 exhibits; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's basically right. With regard to witnesses, we have 52 live witnesses and 43 Rule 92 bis witnesses. A number of further witnesses has been interviewed after the filing of the Prosecution pre-trial brief. I'm talking about four live witnesses and two Rule 92 bis witnesses. These witnesses will be added to our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Four live --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Four live witnesses and two Rule 92 bis witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that is 101 in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: One hundred one in total. However, you as the Defence, must be aware that we will interview further witnesses. I'm talking about a number in the range of between five and ten further witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that will be in total around between 106 and 111.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. The Trial Chamber would encourage the Prosecution to stick with those numbers, and even further, to reduce -- to be able to reduce those numbers, circumstances permitting. I would like to -- I will advise this Trial Chamber not to allow additional documents -- or additional witnesses unless good causes, good reasons, are shown. About the exhibits. You indicate there are about 1.000 exhibits during the course of the earlier Status Conferences, and is it that it's reduced to 131?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It's somewhere in the middle, Your Honour. As you know, our exhibit list, the current exhibit list, contains 131 exhibits. A number of further exhibits will be added. We are anticipating that we will not reach the number of 1.000 at all. We were able to diminish the number of potential exhibits. It's still hard to predict. However, we can anticipate that at the very end we are talking about 200 to 300, maybe 350 exhibits, but again it's very hard to predict at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have those potential exhibits been disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: As I already mentioned, since mid-May there was no opportunity at all to disclose materials to the Defence since the then-Defence counsel Mr. Soyer, due to the lack of cooperation with his client, wasn't prepared to receive materials. We have put together a number of binders we wish to disclose to the current Defence counsel. We offered these binders yesterday. However, for obvious reasons, he's not able to carry them, so we will send these binders by mail. These binders contain the 131 documents as listed in the exhibit list. These documents are available since the date of the filing of the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief. They haven't been picked up by Defence counsel. So far we will also disclose some further exhibits, and in future additional exhibits will follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it was agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It was agreed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. And I wonder what happened to the so-called Sarajevo collection or materials provided by the Bosnian authorities from official archives. The Prosecution indicated that it would be able to complete this review by the date set for submission of pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Sarajevo collection, as you may know, is a collection comprised of some 50.000 pages of documents. There are a number of documents from the Sarajevo collection that form part of the current exhibit list. However, the Sarajevo collection as such is not the problem. The problem is that we are still getting materials from the BiH side. It's basically not a problem. It's a fact that we get such materials. These materials have to be sifted through, and they have to be analysed, and finally a decision has to be made as to whether the Prosecution wants to use them as exhibits. This is an ongoing process, and I can't tell you at this point in time an end date once we will be able to finish such a procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. But 92 bis statements, what is the status in relation to that evidence in terms of certification and disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We are very well advanced in this regard, Your Honour. Almost all statements the Prosecution intends to use as Rule 92 bis witness statements are certified. Meanwhile, they have been certified since April 2002. Translation of such amendments to statements is currently in progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So they are included in the disclosure package which you mentioned just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: But not the translations. The translations of amendments are in progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I remember that, Mr. Withopf, you indicated during the earlier Status Conference and Rule 65 ter Conference that massive JNA manuals are yet to be translated and thus the military expert report would not be available until August or early September. And it was also suggested that the Prosecution might need to submit an addendum to its pre-trial brief according to the outcome of the military expert report. What is the current situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just to give you a brief update. The relevant portion or the portions that the Prosecution considers to be relevant meanwhile have been translated. The military expert has been provided with such translations. We had a number of meetings with the Prosecution military expert. The assistance of the military expert is meanwhile well advanced. Some preliminary working documents have been provided by the expert. However, to date we didn't have -- we didn't get the final report. The final report can be expected within the first month of next year. However, I must say depending on the outcome of the final expert report, the Prosecution may have to amend or to file an addendum to its pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or may not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Or may not, depending on the outcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And it was also indicated that two doctors carrying out the postmortem examination would be served as expert reports upon the Defence. Could you give any observation on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes. We have two pathologists who did the post-mortem reports. Obviously these two doctors can be considered as experts at well. Their reports are currently available in summary translation only. The full translation of such experts' reports will be requested in the very near future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When do you think the full translation will be ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These documents are very comprehensive documents. It depends on the situation within CLSS. It's hard to anticipate. It may last six weeks, eight weeks, 12 weeks. It's hard to predict. A summary translation, however, already exists, and the summary translation can be disclosed if the Defence wishes them to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will consider whether to put a time limit after having heard the Defence's comment on that later. So in light of all that was discussed up to now today, how long does the Prosecution estimate its case to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That's a question, Your Honour, we have been asked several times in the course of the previous meetings. Again, I basically have to say it depends very much on further agreements with the Defence, obviously. Mr. Caglar, yesterday, mentioned that he doesn't feel himself bound to the previous stipulations. That may have a negative effect, a negative impact on the length of the trial. However, the Prosecution estimates the Prosecution case being finished within four to six months, considering the number of live witnesses we intend to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. I now turn to the Defence. I'm very pleased to hear, Mr. Caglar, to hear from you that you will be able to produce the Defence pre-trial brief at the end of -- by the end of this year. So I would encourage the Defence to meet that deadline in any way. As Mr. Withopf, the Prosecutor, raised the issue, Mrs. Kreho and Mr. Halilovic jointly tendered a document named Summary of the Defence pre-trial brief on 22nd July of this year. So would the forthcoming pre-trial brief go along with the same line that was suggested in the summary brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the summary you are referring to was prepared by me. Actually, the broad lines of the Defence are very simple. I think that we need to develop the main lines of that defence which will be summarised for you, and I intend to follow along the same lines in my defence. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. One thing to be pointed out in relation to this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apology again. One thing to be pointed out in relation to this is the following: The final paragraph of that document summary brief states, I quote: "The Defence submits that a reasonable trier cannot conclude that the accused is criminally responsible as a superior and requests that the accused be acquitted in a reasonable time limit." And then Prosecution responded that "Should this request be considered to be a motion for judgement of acquittal under Rule 98 of the Rules, then the motion should be denied for being premature." However, as the document in which the Defence's request was made was entitled "Summary," and because Rule 98 clearly only permits a motion for judgement of acquittal to be made at the close of the Prosecution's case, this Chamber took the view that this was not a serious application to be considered. Mr. Caglar, do you have any observation about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right, Your Honour. This is something for later. This was just the proposal, and we will see as things progress. It is not a proposal to be addressed immediately. It is no more than a proposal to take note of, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And according to the summary brief of the Defence pre-trial brief, the main point of the Defence case seemed to me that the accused was not in the command position and did not have effective or material control over the forces on the ground. Am I right in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then may I take it then the Defence will not vigorously and seriously challenge the fact that such crimes as alleged in the indictment had been actually committed?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I have just said, this is merely a little summary. I am not fully in command of the whole brief or the arguments which have been developed by the Prosecutor. I'm familiar with them only partially, and at this stage of the debate, I cannot give you a precise answer, nor can I convey my ideas which I haven't had time to develop. I need time. There are certainly other arguments that will be submitted, and I reserve the right to develop my ideas in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course the Defence position is fully understandable. And one last thing again is that -- it's related to agreed facts. During Mr. Balijagic's period as Defence counsel, the Defence was able to agree to a set of stipulated facts. What would be your observations, and there is any possibility of agreeing any further stipulated facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, allow me to do that a little later on, please, because I haven't fully been able to study the document that I have been served with. The time hasn't allowed for that. Maybe within two or three weeks I will be able to give you a more precise answer. And I don't think that my opinion will change in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I would only recommend that -- to try to recommend you to put -- as much as possible to put them in writing in the pre-trial brief, as much as possible and as specifically as possible. I think I dealt with some -- most of the outstanding matters, but are there any issues to raise at this moment? Any party. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is nothing to add from the Prosecution's side. However, the Prosecution would very strongly urge or would like to very strongly urge the Senior Legal Officer assigned to this case to convene a Rule 65 ter Conference in some near future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That's exactly what I had in mind. For the Defence are there any issues to raise at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAGLAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not for the moment, Your Honour. Not just yet, Your Honour. I have no other questions to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I would like to recommend the parties to contact our Senior Legal Officer, and I think the time would be, in my opinion, mid or -- from mid to late November will be suitable for the parties. And before that -- or the Defence also, I would recommend the Defence to contact the Prosecutor to discuss the matter relating to the disclosure issues, and other things may be discussed at the 65 ter Conference in one month's time from now. I think I'm very -- I will expect to have a -- to receive the pre-trial brief from the Defence at the end of this year, and then I will consider either to have a Pre-Trial Conference then or the -- another Status Conference. So in case we decided to have a Pre-Trial Conference, I will have the Senior Legal Officer to hold another 65 ter Conference before that Pre-Trial Conference which may take place in mid-January next year. And if I decided to have another Status Conference to coordinate some more issues, that will also take place at the same time, around -- at the end of January next year. Unless there are any other matters to raise at this moment? So this Status Conference is adjourned.
